props.title: Confederate States of America

sections.content: Confederate States of America (2004) delivers one of mockumentary's most audacious alternate histories by imagining a world where the South won the Civil War. Director Kevin Willmott crafts this provocative film as a British documentary being broadcast on Confederate television, complete with disturbing fictional commercials for slave-related products. It shares DNA with The Blair Witch Project (1999) and District 9 (2009) in using fake documentary techniques to explore charged social issues, but pushes even further by maintaining its unsettling premise across decades of reimagined American history.

sections.content: What makes CSA particularly effective is how it uses real historical artifacts and events, twisting them just enough to create its alternate timeline. Like Death of a President (2006) and Good Bye, Lenin! (2003), it manipulates archival footage and familiar documentary techniques to craft a convincing alternate reality. The film's genius lies in showing how many actual racist policies and products from our real history could easily fit into its imagined Confederate victory timeline.

The mockumentary format allows Willmott to examine how media shapes historical narratives, similar to Zelig (1983) and C.S.A. borrows techniques from Ken Burns' landmark The Civil War (1990) documentary series. But where those films use the format to illuminate truth, CSA weaponizes it to expose how easily media can normalize oppression through entertainment and advertising. SUBHEAD: Alternative History as Social Commentary

movies.title: BlacKkKlansman
movies.slug: Spike Lee's based-on-truth story about a Black cop infiltrating the KKK

sections.content: CSA belongs to a vital tradition of speculative films that use alternate history to critique present-day society, including The Man in the High Castle (2015-2019) and Inglourious Basterds (2009). These works understand that sometimes the best way to examine difficult truths about our actual history is through the lens of "what if?" scenarios. The film's fake commercials for modern-day slave-tracking systems and Confederate-approved products hit especially hard because they're only slightly exaggerated versions of real historical advertisements.
